original_value: Air pollution is a global problem and can be perceived as a modern-day curse. One way of dealing with it is by finding economical ways to monitor and forecast air quality. Accurately monitoring and forecasting fine particulate matter (PM2.5) concentrations is a challenging prediction task but Internet of Things (IoT) can help in developing economical and agile ways to design such systems. In this paper, we use a historical data-based approach to perform PM2.5 forecasting. A forecasting method is developed which uses exponential smoothing with drift. Experiments and evaluation were performed using the real-time PM2.5 data obtained from large scale deployment of IoT devices in Taichung region in Taiwan. We used the data from 132 monitoring stations to evaluate our model’s performance. A comparison of prediction accuracy and computation time between the proposed model and three widely used forecasting models was done. The results suggest that our method can perform PM2.5 forecast for 132 monitoring stations with error as low as 0.16    μ   g/    m 3     and also with an acceptable computation time of 30 s. Further evaluation was done by forecasting PM2.5 for next 3 h. The results show that 90 % of the monitoring stations have error under 1.5    μ   g/    m 3     which is significantly low.

result.paraphrase: Air pollution is a worldwide issue and can be regarded as a modern-day curse. A practical response is to develop economical methods for monitoring and forecasting air quality. Reliable PM2.5 concentration monitoring and prediction is difficult, but the Internet of Things (IoT) can support the creation of low-cost, agile systems for this purpose. In this paper, we present a historical-data-based approach to PM2.5 forecasting. The proposed forecasting method uses exponential smoothing with drift. Experiments and evaluation were carried out using real-time PM2.5 data from a large-scale IoT deployment in the Taichung region of Taiwan. Data from 132 monitoring stations were used to assess model performance. We compared prediction accuracy and computation time for the proposed model against three widely used forecasting models. The results indicate that the method can forecast PM2.5 for 132 monitoring stations with error as low as 0.16 μg/m3 and an acceptable computation time of 30 s. We also evaluated next-3-h PM2.5 forecasting. The results show that 90% of the monitoring stations achieve error below 1.5 μg/m3, which is very low.
